title: Is Beauty in the Eye of the Beholder?
objective: After this level you can weigh Hume's standard of taste against Kant's claim that a judgment of beauty speaks for everyone.
summary: Hume: beauty lives in feeling, but true critics’ joint verdict sets a standard. Kant: calling something beautiful claims everyone’s agreement. Each view faces an objection.

cards.headline: You love a song. Your friend can’t stand it. Is either of you wrong?
cards.body: Most people shrug: beauty is in the eye of the beholder. David Hume and Immanuel Kant weren’t satisfied with the shrug, and they disagreed about what should replace it.

cards.headline: Beauty lives in the feeling
cards.body: In “Of the Standard of Taste” (1757), Hume agreed that beauty is not a quality in objects: it belongs entirely to our feelings. Yet he refused to call every verdict equal. Rating the forgotten poet Ogilby as highly as Milton, he wrote, is like calling a molehill as high as a mountain, and we rightly call such taste absurd. So some feelings are better guides than others. The question is whose.

cards.headline: The key in the barrel
cards.body: Hume answers with a story. Two of Sancho’s kinsmen taste a barrel of wine. One praises it but detects a hint of leather; the other, a hint of iron. Everyone mocks them, until the barrel is emptied and an old key on a leather strap turns up at the bottom. True critics are like those tasters, Hume said: strong sense, delicate feeling, practice, comparison, no prejudice. Their joint verdict is the standard of taste.

cards.headline: Kant: beauty speaks for everyone
cards.body: Kant, in his Critique of Judgment (1790), drew a sharper line. Call Canary wine pleasant and you should really say “pleasant to me”; nobody need argue. But call a poem beautiful and you judge “not merely for himself, but for every one”, with a universal voice. No rule or proof can force others to agree, yet you expect it. And the pleasure, Kant held, is disinterested: it involves no desire.

mascot.line: People mix these up: “pleasant to me” is a report on you, while “beautiful” asks everyone to agree.

cards.headline: Each side’s weak spot
cards.body: Critics find a circle in Hume: great art is what true critics approve, but true critics are picked out by approving great art. Kant has critics too. Nietzsche attacked the idea that pleasure in beauty is free of desire, calling pleasure cut off from our passionate lives unrealistic. The debate is still open.

cards.headline: Is Beauty in the Eye of the Beholder?: the big picture
learned: True critics’ joint verdict sets the standard
Each view faces a serious objection

questions.prompt: In Hume’s story about Sancho’s kinsmen, what was found at the bottom of the wine barrel?

options.label: A rusty iron nail with a cork
options.rationale: Iron was only one of the tastes.

options.label: An old key on a leather strap
A small chunk of rusted iron

questions.explanation: An old key on a leather thong explained both the leather and the iron: the delicate tasters were right.

questions.prompt: A friend says, “This painting is beautiful, but that’s just me.” What would Kant find odd about this?

options.label: Only trained experts may call things beautiful
options.rationale: Kant doesn’t limit it to experts.

options.label: Beauty can be measured with instruments
options.rationale: No rule or proof settles beauty for Kant.

options.label: Calling it beautiful already claims everyone’s agreement
Paintings can only ever be pleasant
options.rationale: Kant’s examples of beauty include poems.

questions.explanation: For Kant, “pleasant to me” is private, but “beautiful” speaks with a universal voice, so “just me” takes back the claim.

questions.prompt: Hume and Kant argue about whether judgments of beauty can be correct. Which branch of philosophy from Level 2 is that debate part of?

options.label: Epistemology
options.rationale: It’s about beauty, not knowledge in general.

questions.explanation: Aesthetics is the theory of beauty and, more broadly, the philosophy of art.
